Tech Report: Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.
  • According to recent reports, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just introduced its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim.
  • Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.

According to recent reports, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just introduced its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim. Meanwhile, ALSO, the high-tech electric bicycle startup spun out of Rivian, revealed that it was halting deliveries of its futuristic TM-B electric bicycle amid mounting software problems.

Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical. Both have deep engineering roots and were incubated by successful technology companies. And both have developed impressive proprietary systems that set their bikes apart from the competition.

But their dramatically different launches offer an interesting lesson about the difference between innovation and execution, and which has proven to be more successful in the real world.

Amflow’s story actually begins before the brand debuted its first electric mountain bike.

DJI, the Chinese drone giant, had spent years perfecting the art of building small, lightweight, powerful electric motors, sophisticated electronic controllers, and advanced battery management systems. Those are all technologies that translate remarkably well to electric bicycles, even if the applications are quite different.

That expertise helped give rise to the Avinox e-bike drive system, which quickly earned a reputation as one of the most impressive electric bicycle drivetrains on the market. The mid-drive motor and control system rapidly ate away at the huge market share long held by Bosch and other leaders.

The motors offered an almost ridiculous amount of power in a lightweight package, paired with sophisticated sensors and software that delivered smooth, natural-feeling pedal assistance. The system was also designed as a tightly integrated ecosystem, with displays, controllers, batteries, and motors working together.

Amflow’s first electric mountain bikes demonstrated just how well that technology could work in the real world.

And now, with the launch of the new Amflow UE commuter series, the company is taking that proven technology and applying it to an entirely different kind of riding.

The latest bikes bring Avinox’s powerful pedal assistance and intelligent electronic controls to a more practical urban platform, adding commuter-focused features designed to make everyday riding more convenient.

There’s plenty of proprietary technology here, but perhaps the most crucial thing about Amflow’s approach is what the company didn’t reinvent.

The bikes still fundamentally work like bicycles.

You pedal, a conventional mechanical drivetrain transfers that power to the rear wheel, and an electric motor provides assistance. It’s the same basic arrangement that has worked on electric bicycles for decades, just refined with much more advanced engineering.

It has been revealed that amflow didn’t need to fundamentally change the bicycle to make it feel futuristic. Instead, the tech giant focused on making the familiar bicycle experience better.

It has been revealed that and while the new commuter models are still too fresh to judge their long-term reliability, early impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. That’s an encouraging start, especially considering the manufacturer’s already established reputation in the demanding electric mountain bike market.

ALSO, on the other hand, took a dramatically different approach.

The firm emerged from Rivian, the American electric vehicle manufacturer known for its technologically advanced electric trucks and SUVs.

It has been revealed that like DJI, Rivian has extensive experience developing sophisticated electric drivetrains, battery systems, power electronics, and software. And like Amflow, ALSO wanted to bring that expertise to a upcoming generation of electric bicycles.

But instead of using those technologies to improve a conventional bicycle, ALSO decided to rethink the entire machine.

It has been revealed that the company’s TM-B electric bicycle uses a pedal-by-wire system, meaning the pedals aren’t mechanically connected to the rear wheel. Instead, pedaling turns a generator that sends data signals and power through an electronic system, while software determines how the rear motor responds.

Pedal-by-wire systems have some genuine potential advantages. They can eliminate traditional chains, belts, derailleurs, and other mechanical drivetrain components, which has helped land them on many unconventional e-bikes such as extremely long cargo e-bikes and truck-like electric bicycles that would otherwise require ridiculously long chain runs.

They can also allow engineers to completely customize the relationship between pedaling effort and motor response, creating riding experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a conventional bicycle drivetrain.

It has been revealed that but there’s a catch. When you replace a relatively simple mechanical system with a sophisticated electronic one, you’re also introducing a lot more opportunities for things to go wrong.

And unlike a conventional bicycle, where many drivetrain problems can be diagnosed and repaired with basic tools, a highly proprietary software-defined bicycle can become much more dependent on its manufacturer to keep it running.

That’s not inherently a bad tradeoff. Modern electric cars have demonstrated that software-defined vehicles can offer tremendous benefits. But it puts enormous pressure on the manufacturer to get the hardware, software, and integration right.

Unfortunately, ALSO’s early rollout suggests that the manufacturer hasn’t quite managed that yet.

The contrast between the two companies became particularly striking last week.

Amflow unveiled its new commuter models, building on the reputation of its successful electric mountain bikes and earning enthusiastic early reviews.

ALSO, meanwhile, confirmed that it was pausing deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycle due to software-related issues. That’s on top of earlier delivery delays and reports of customers having to send their new ALSO TM-B bicycles back for repairs.

We’ve also previously reported on some unusual charging and discharging behavior with the TM-B, raising questions about how the bike’s sophisticated electronic systems were managing energy. Those concerns now look particularly relevant in light of the company’s latest announcement.

To be fair, we don’t know how widespread the problems are across ALSO’s delivered bicycles, and it’s entirely possible that the manufacturer will resolve these issues relatively quickly with updates on delivered bikes and reflashing software on bikes yet to be shipped.

It has been revealed that nor should we assume that Amflow’s new commuter bikes will be trouble-free simply because their initial reviews are positive. Long-term reliability is something that can only be established over time. But the difference in their respective launches is hard to ignore.

In a recent development, both are examples of tech-focused startups attempting to reinvent the future of e-bikes. One company is expanding its lineup after successfully establishing its technology in the market. The other is struggling to get its first product consistently into customers’ hands.

And that brings us to what I think is the most interesting part of this story.

There’s a fundamental difference between developing impressive technology and successfully turning that technology into a dependable consumer product.

Both Amflow and ALSO have accomplished the first part.

The engineering behind the Avinox drive system is genuinely impressive, and the TM-B’s pedal-by-wire architecture is one of the more ambitious attempts to rethink the electric bicycle in recent years.

But Amflow appears to have taken a more measured approach to bringing that technology to consumers.

The organization first developed and refined a sophisticated electric bicycle drivetrain, proved it in the demanding electric mountain bike market, and then adapted it to commuter applications.

ALSO attempted something much more ambitious right out of the gate: launching an entirely newly introduced bicycle architecture with numerous interdependent proprietary systems.

In a recent development, neither approach is inherently wrong. In fact, if nobody ever attempted the latter, we’d probably miss out on some genuinely revolutionary products. But there’s a reason that so many successful technological innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

In a recent development, sometimes the smartest engineering decision isn’t figuring out how to replace something that already works. It’s figuring out how to make it work better.

And there’s a certain irony in the fact that Amflow’s new commuter bike looks relatively ordinary, yet appears to deliver an extraordinary riding experience.

ALSO’s TM-B, meanwhile, looks like something from the future, but its early ownership experience has been considerably less impressive.

I want to be clear that I’m not rooting for or against either manufacturer here.

Recent findings suggest that quite the opposite. Both ALSO and Amflow are working to accelerate the state of the industry. I’ve been fascinated by the TM-B since it was first unveiled, and I genuinely hope the tech giant succeeds. And Amflow has taken the fresh perspective brought by its parent company, DJI, and turned it into real-world progress. The e-bike industry needs more innovation to help push everyone forward.

I love seeing companies take significant swings in the electric bicycle industry, especially when they’re attempting something more interesting than slapping a bigger motor and battery onto an otherwise generic frame.

Sources indicate that and I think pedal-by-wire technology has real potential. The ability to electronically control the relationship between pedaling and propulsion opens up fascinating possibilities, even if it also introduces new challenges.

According to recent reports, I should also mention that I have not personally ridden either of these bikes, and thus this is analysis from the sidelines. The Amflow UE Carbon was only unveiled a few days ago, though I’ve got one on the way and am excited to begin testing it soon and to report back here on the experience. As for ALSO, the bike was unveiled a year ago, and I was slated to be at the launch for test riding, but barely an hour after I posted an exclusive article revealing that ALSO had accidentally leaked its own images of its yet-to-be-unveiled bike on its website, I received an email uninviting me to the upcoming event and test ride.

So keep in mind that all of this is being mentioned as an analyst with nearly two decades in the e-bike industry and hundreds of different e-bikes under my belt, not from personal experience with either bike model.

Recent findings suggest that but as someone who spends an enormous amount of time riding, testing, and working on electric bicycles, I also appreciate the value of simplicity. A bicycle is an inherently elegant machine. It’s lightweight, efficient, relatively easy to maintain, and remarkably dependable considering how few components it needs to function.

Electric assistance has already made that machine dramatically more useful for millions of people. The question is how much more complexity we should introduce in pursuit of further improvements.

Amflow seems to be asking, “How can we use advanced technology to make riding a bicycle better?”.

ALSO seems to be asking, “What if we could completely rethink how a bicycle works?”.

Both are worthwhile questions, and I’m glad there are companies pursuing both answers. But right now, Amflow is demonstrating the advantages of building on a proven foundation, while ALSO is learning some painful lessons about the challenges of reinventing the wheel.

It's pretty clear that electric cars are much simpler than ICE cars, and I would argue this is an advantage. However, the same cannot be noted for the ALSO bike. It's much more complicated than a normal bike, or even a normal e-bike. It seems like an answer in search of a problem.

And perhaps that’s the biggest takeaway from this tale of two high-tech e-bike startups.

The future of electric bicycles will undoubtedly involve more sophisticated motors, batteries, sensors, and software. But the companies that succeed won’t necessarily be the ones that pack the most technology into their bikes.

They’ll be the ones that figure out how to make all that technology work so seamlessly that riders barely have to think about it.

Because at the end of the day, the best electric bicycle isn’t necessarily the one with the most advanced technology. It’s the one that makes you want to ride it every day – and actually lets you.

After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events.
  • Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.
  • There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a newly introduced world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Sources indicate that ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a fresh Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

Industry observers note that at the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Industry observers note that swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Recent findings suggest that then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

Recent findings suggest that the aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Industry observers note that of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

Recent findings suggest that in November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing fresh free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

In a recent development, while you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free patch, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alfa Romeo and Maserati each have plenty of history they can leverage.
  • Sources indicate that on November 23, Stellantis unveiled that it was ending its participation in the World Endurance Championship at the end of this year; next year, it'll end its efforts in Formula E once the season is over.
  • It has been revealed that perhaps most notably, Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy affected employees, including into performance-car development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alfa Romeo and Maserati each have plenty of history they can leverage. Getting American buyers excited to snap up what's current or excited about what’s next has proven much harder, though. Now, a retreat by Stellantis from motorsport could give both brands the engineering attention they need.

Sources indicate that on November 23, Stellantis unveiled that it was ending its participation in the World Endurance Championship at the end of this year; next year, it'll end its efforts in Formula E once the season is over. Its new priorities are customer racing and high-performance vehicle development. Alfa Romeo and Maserati are explicitly named as beneficiaries of that expertise.

It has been revealed that perhaps most notably, Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy affected employees, including into performance-car development. That could put people accustomed to solving problems at the highest end of motorsport into roles where they help customers enjoy their cars on public roads.

Sources indicate that there's certainly plenty for these brands to do on that front. Alfa Romeo sold just 2316 vehicles in the United States through September, down 52 percent from the same period last year. Its third-quarter total was 569 cars across the Giulia, Stelvio, and Tonale. Whatever affection Americans might have for the badge, it isn’t translating into much showroom traffic.

Maserati, meanwhile, has fresh material to work with; its updated North American lineup includes a 385-hp Grecale V-6, and 582-hp Trofeo versions of the GranTurismo and GranCabrio. Those are solid offerings, but when it comes to marketing, there's plenty of room for the brand to grow.

Of course, there’s a sizable financial caveat: Stellantis hasn’t disclosed expected savings from the withdrawals or promised an accompanying increase in, for example, American marketing spending. It reported a €453 million ($497 million) net loss and negative industrial free cash flow of roughly €4 billion ($4.4 billion) in the third quarter. Any freed-up cash will have plenty of competing demands. That said, it's great to see that Stellantis directly emphasizing that the end of the WEC and Formula E programs will mean more resources go to Alfa and Maserati production cars—and “high-performance models” at that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

According to recent reports, before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

Recent findings suggest that with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to Fresh York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most notable video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

According to recent reports, taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this very month, Jensen Huang, CEO of the world’s leading chip producer, Nvidia, not to mention one of the most crucial companies to the advancement of gaming as a creator of GPUs, was wracked with controversy. Huang admitted an affair with a woman alleged to be a spy for the Chinese government and was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive, according to the BBC.

Industry observers note that following all of these revelations, Huang voluntarily resigned from his position as CEO. For a brief, glorious moment, the gaming community breathed a sigh of relief, as it was Huang’s gung-ho attitude on AI-centric developments over all else that had largely contributed to Nvidia shifting focus away from gaming hardware. Maybe we’d start seeing affordable, optimized GPUs again!

Unfortunately, we are not allowed to have nice things in this timeline. According to a BBC report this morning, following a unanimous vote from the current Nvidia corporate board, Huang has been officially reinstated to his position as CEO. Yay.

According to the BBC report, despite previous insistences from the board that Huang would not be reinstated to his position, the ultimate conclusion that they came to is that only Huang could continue the AI-focused push Nvidia has been running with lately.

"The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," the board’s current chair said in a public statement on the Nvidia website.

The ultimate conclusion that they came to is that only Huang could continue the AI-focused push Nvidia has been running with lately.

Apparently, Huang’s return was orchestrated at least in part by United States President Donald Trump, who, in a brief interview with CNBC, said that he “felt very strongly that [Huang] should come back, and we've done a very thorough investigation.

"And the investigation showed that he did - I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents - but he did nothing wrong other than he created a chip that's invaluable.".

Following news of Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia’s stock value bounced up 32%, a notable increase following a 13% drop-off at the end of last week.

In a personal statement on the Nvidia website, Huang remarked that he is “honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a latest industrial revolution.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Recent findings suggest that some analysts speculate that, particularly within the AI-centric tech field, figureheads have become an important part of the push. Parallels have been drawn between Huang’s reinstatement and that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was reinstated in his own position just five days after being fired from it in 2023.

The BBC’s tech and AI analyst Zoe Kleinman posited on the matter, saying that “It indicates a lot that despite the serious accusations made about him and his affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy, ultimately his position in the tech industry has proved to be more notable:.

“There had been many calls for him to be reinstated - including from within the UK House of Lords - on the grounds that the AI industry would be weaker without him.”.

Sources indicate that whatever the precise reason, it’s probably a safe bet that Nvidia will promptly resume its previous course, which means those of us in the gaming sphere won’t be seeing any affordable GPUs any time soon. Oh well, it was nice to dream of a world where you didn't need to justify buying a top-shelf graphics card...

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone who has ever tried to eat lunch sitting in the driver’s seat while parked—or worse yet, flip open a laptop to catch up on emails—knows that a steering wheel takes up a surprisingly large amount of real estate. Thus, manufacturers of all kinds have come up with various steering solutions that have largely remained conceptual, cool show-off pieces for the auto show circuit but little more. Chinese manufacturer BYD just stuck one in a mainstream SUV.

Sources indicate that the Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 is a large six-seater SUV that’s about the size of an Infiniti QX80, with prices starting at the equivalent of $41K in the Chinese market. It’s not a pure EV, but rather a series plug-in hybrid with a 150-hp 1.5-liter turbo four-cylinder acting as a generator to power the 66-kWh battery pack; the dual electric motors combine for 536 hp.Fang Cheng Bao is one of BYD’s subbrands, aimed at delivering an off-road-ready flair. The Tai 9 is certainly a chunky-looking thing, but what’s perhaps most interesting about the top trim level is how it behaves when parked.

See all results for used cars for sale near 32810.

According to recent reports, spend the equivalent of $49K for the highest-grade Tai 9, and you get a folding steering wheel that disappears into the dash. Because the vehicle is entirely steer-by-wire, a technology that only became legal in China less than six months ago, the Tai 9 has no steering column geometry to worry about. The rim splits in half, folds back over the column, and the whole thing retracts, airbag still facing forward.Paired with a driver’s seat that reclines almost completely flat, the appeal here is to provide a more spacious place to relax or work while you charge. Again, this feature is only available when parked, so you can’t retract the wheel while using the Tai 9’s driver-assistance functions.

However, this folding steering wheel does show how car interiors might look for vehicles with Level 4-or-higher autonomy, ones that can operate completely without human intervention in certain cases. On a geofenced section of highway, with automated cruise control activated, you could simply pack your steering wheel away for extra room.

According to recent reports, obviously, driving enthusiasts who obsess over steering feel aren’t going to be too happy about the proliferation of steering-by-wire, never mind having the steering wheel fold away entirely. However, it’s not like a three-ton, three-row PHEV SUV is going to feel like piloting a Caterham anyway.

Recent findings suggest that what’s perhaps most impressive of all is the speed at which BYD managed to get its folding steering wheel technology into the hands of the public, considering the regulatory requirements only came into being months ago. Combined with the firm’s production-car speed record under its Yangwang performance brand, and the sub-$10K price of its Seagull entry-level EV, BYD is certainly active in all segments of the market. Watch this space to see what it gets up to next.

BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.
  • BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France.
  • It has been revealed that the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.

BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France. If it closes, it would be the Chinese giant’s second passenger car factory in the EU after Hungary, and the first time a Chinese automaker buys an existing car plant in Europe.

It has been revealed that the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up. Alongside the announcement, Ineos Automotive mentioned it looks to move Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the US, which it says accounts for about 70% of its sales. It has shortlisted US sites, hasn’t named any, and is aiming to start production there in 2028.

The math is simple. Every Grenadier shipped from France to the US gets hit with a 15% tariff, and the Quartermaster pickup falls under the 25% tariff on imported pickups. When 7 out of 10 of your customers are American, building your trucks in Lorraine stops making sense.

Ineos notes it will keep building both models at Hambach “for the medium term” if the sale goes through, so the two companies would share the site for a while.

Industry observers note that neither side disclosed a price or a closing date, and the sale still has to go through consultation with employee representatives. BYD will soon find out that France is nothing like China when it comes to employee representation. There’s also no word yet on which BYD models would come out of Hambach or when. Same for the plant’s roughly 1,000 employees: BYD made no commitment on how many it would keep.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li mentioned the tech giant wants to give European consumers “vehicles built in France” that use BYD’s technology.

Recent findings suggest that hambach opened in 1997 as “Smartville,” Mercedes’ factory for the Smart Fortwo, and it later built the all-electric Smart EQ Fortwo. Ineos bought it from Mercedes at the end of 2020 after dropping its plan to build a fresh factory in Wales, and Grenadier production started in 2022. Ineos says it has put nearly €540 million into the site since 2019.

Recent findings suggest that capacity is about 30,000 Grenadiers a year. That’s not much by BYD’s standards. BYD sold 3,561,615 passenger vehicles globally in the first 10 months of the year, which means 30,000 units is less than three days of its output.

Industry observers note that there’s also a bit of irony in who’s buying. Ineos unveiled its first EV, the Fusilier, in early 2024 while romanticizing gas cars at the same event. A few months later, it shelved the electric model indefinitely, blaming “reluctant consumer uptake” of EVs. Now it’s selling its only factory to the world’s largest EV maker.

Sources indicate that this isn’t a surprise. Back in May, Stella Li said BYD was in talks with Stellantis and “other companies too” to take over underused plants in Europe, and that BYD would rather own and run a plant than form a joint venture. Hambach fits that description exactly.

BYD’s first European car plant, in Szeged, Hungary, started trial production earlier this year and is expected to reach mass production in early 2027, with the Dolphin Surf and Atto 2 first in line. BYD eventually wants more than 150,000 vehicles a year out of it. Its separate factory project in Turkey has been put on pause.

The motivation is regulatory. China-built BYD EVs face a 17% countervailing duty in the EU on top of the standard 10% car tariff, imported Chinese hybrids are now subject to quotas, and the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules would tie EV subsidies and public contracts to how much of a vehicle is built locally. A French plant solves a lot of those problems at once.

And BYD isn’t alone. Leapmotor started building the B10 at Stellantis’ Zaragoza plant in Spain in October, Dongfeng aims to build cars at a Stellantis factory in France, Geely is reportedly lining up a Ford plant in Spain, and Chery already assembles vehicles in Barcelona.

In a recent development, chery is the one BYD should watch. Through October, BYD registered 320,445 vehicles in Europe, up 133%, according to Automotive News. Chery Group was just ahead with 320,631, up 235%. A gap of 186 cars.

Europe matters more than ever for BYD because home isn’t going well. BYD brand sales in China fell 40% to 1,544,699 vehicles over the first 10 months, and its global passenger vehicle sales are down 2.7%.

According to recent reports, this is a smart, cheap move for BYD. Building Szeged took years, including land disputes with private owners. Hambach comes with a trained workforce, a paint shop, a supplier base on the German border, and a seller that’s motivated to leave. You don’t get a much easier entry into France, but the easiest in France is still probably more difficult than anything BYD faced in China when it comes to deploying newly introduced production capacity.

According to recent reports, the 30,000-unit capacity is small, but BYD isn’t buying it for what it builds today. It’s buying a “Made in France” label ahead of local content rules.

I'm guessing BYD is gambling on the French not making it too difficult as it would deter future investment. They're probably also going to use a lot of robots.

We also can’t ignore the symmetry here. Ineos is leaving Europe to build in the US because of tariffs. BYD is buying into Europe because of tariffs. That’s protectionism moving factories. Europe keeps the jobs, and the workers who used to build Smart EVs might get to build EVs again.

And yes, it’s funny that BYD is moving into the home of the Grenadier, a vehicle that exists because Ratcliffe loved the old Defender, days after a court in The Hague barred BYD’s Ti7 from the EU for infringing Land Rover’s Defender design.

According to recent reports, the real question is what BYD puts on the line in Hambach. If it’s battery-electric cars, great. If it’s plug-in hybrids built to get around quotas, Europe is trading one gas-burning 4×4 factory for another.

The Improbable Success of a ‘Poky Little Motoring Show’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • Recent findings suggest that in fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time. High-resolution internet video and the streaming revolution were distant spots on the horizon. But the changing landscape unwittingly created the perfect conditions for an accidental phenomenon: a TV show about cars with an estimated global audience of 350 million, a broadcasting triumph that would be impossible to replicate today. Because the Aughts was the decade that seeded the improbable success of a self-confessed “poky little motoring show” called Top Gear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies. The series added Jeremy Clarkson to its hosting lineup in 1988 to bring a bit of wit to what was still a fundamentally earnest format. In 1999, he left the show, and two years later, the BBC announced that Top Gear was going to be “rested,” a polite British way of saying “canceled.”.

At the same time, Jeremy and an old school friend, TV producer Andy Wilman, who had been a lesser Top Gear presenter, were working on plans for a bigger, more boisterous car show called Carmageddon. When the pair pitched it to the head of the BBC Two channel, she liked the idea and agreed to commission the show with one proviso: Carmageddon should become a reboot of Top Gear. The fuse had been lit, but free­wheeling global success wasn’t the master proposal. In fact, there was no grand scheme, only a vague hope to make a halfway-­decent show for audiences in the U.K. I know this because from 2002 to 2015, I was Top Gear’s script editor.

This, like so much of the show, was something of an accident. I’d worked briefly with Jeremy on the old version of Top Gear, and he’d liked my satirical car website, Sniff Petrol, but if I hadn’t bumped into him in a restaurant and been invited to “come in for a chat,” perhaps the opportunity would have passed me by. As it is, I went to see Jeremy and Andy, and I listened to their ideas, many of which sounded strange. A racing driver who couldn’t tell you anything about a car because he never spoke? A segment forcing celebrities to drive around a track in a low-budget grocery getter? An indoor studio for a car show? Hmm. But Jeremy and Andy are persuasive people, and I agreed to join nonetheless.

We auditioned a lot of people to co-host and eventually found Richard Hammond, a car journalist who performed an unremarkable screen test but then reduced us to hysterics with self-deprecating stories as he was walking toward the exit.

We made a pilot episode, which was a disaster, then a second pilot episode, which was also a disaster, after which point there was no time to try again because we had a scheduled on-air date. We’d go to the pub after work and sit there making despairing sighs and ask, “What are we doing?” We were not plotting world domination. Our biggest goal was to get a show out on time so the BBC didn’t have to broadcast reruns instead.

But we were allowed to carry on, and our first season attracted modest viewing figures, just passing the low target the BBC had issued. Back then, some broadcasters were willing to nurture shows and let them grow gently rather than demanding instant success.

Top Gear needed this patience because it often felt like we were making it up as we went along. In the popular consciousness, the show is remembered for Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May driving malfunctioning cars across harsh and distant lands. But it didn’t start like that at all. We didn’t have James in season one (BBC management thought he was too similar to Jeremy); instead, a car dealer called Jason Dawe was in the third spot. We didn’t go abroad because we were a British show and thought we should film in the U.K., no matter how gray and rainy it might be. We didn’t put the three hosts together in the field until the fourth season, an experiment that yielded nuggets of gold. We never planned to create epic road trips occupying entire shows, until a journey across the Southern United States generated too much material to squeeze into a 20-minute film and was allowed to roam free as an hour-long special.

Recent findings suggest that what we did have from the start was a certain editorial rigor. Jeremy began his career as a local newspaper journalist. Richard had a background in live radio. James worked on car magazines for years. They’d grown up in worlds that demanded quick thinking and an endless supply of ideas. Sometimes Jeremy would stride into the office booming, “I’ve had a thought . . . .” Sometimes we’d sit around, batting stupid notions back and forth.

Recent findings suggest that as part of my job, I’d scribble down what we mentioned, then try to hack the best bits into something workable. After that came the important part. Any idea, no matter how brilliant it first seemed, was then poked and prodded and dismantled to make sure it was as good as it could be. When we had a full episode’s worth of vetted ideas, I’d sit down with one or all of the presenters, and we’d write a script. For a solo track test, this would be detailed and extensive. For a three-header out in the field, the introduction would be tightly written to make sure our mission was clear, in our minds and to the viewers, after which there would be rough scene headings and perhaps the odd one-liner. As a production team, we’d plan situations and challenges that we thought would allow the hosts to run free with ad-libs and arguing.

Sources indicate that jeremy, Richard, and James were very different people with a love of cars as their common ground. We never had to fake their on-screen personalities; that’s just who they were. Jeremy, bombastic and attention seeking. Richard, excitable and a verbal sniper with killer one-­liners. James, often giving the impression that he’d rather be at home dis­mantling a motorcycle than forced to hang out with these two morons. The dynamic worked.

Recent findings suggest that that such a poorly planned piece of programming eventually found itself a global success is down to the decade in which it was born, a time when people still watched the same show at the same time. One inadvertent stroke of genius was the BBC’s decision to schedule Top Gear on a Sunday evening, traditionally a quiet night on TV in the U.K. Among straight-faced detective demonstrates and florid costume dramas, the hijinks of Top Gear—a nun in a monster truck, a bus jumping motorcycles, a man trying to destroy a To­yota Hilux in increasingly elaborate ways—shone like a beacon of eccentricity. The next morning, everyone could go into work or school and talk about it.

Sources indicate that ratings grew steadily. Then, during filming in 2006 for the ninth season, Richard crashed a jet-­propelled dragster. The show was paused while he recovered from serious injuries. When we returned, viewing figures in the U.K. jumped dramatically.

Global success came later, especially with the growth of YouTube and other social media. ­Suddenly anyone could clip out their favorite bits of Top Gear and make them accessible all around the world. An American gearhead called Alex Mills founded a site called FinalGear, where fans could discuss Top Gear and share BitTorrent links so people everywhere could download the show, if not entirely legally. Top Gear became cult viewing in countries where car shows weren’t trying to turn pickup trucks into boats and a three-wheeled car into a space shuttle. Which was, of course, everywhere else.

It has been revealed that also, the car landscape of the Aughts gave the show great material upon which to build. It was the era of the hypercar, and at its peak was that stats-heavy poster child, the Bugatti Veyron. But it was also a time when Subaru and Mitsubishi were slugging it out to make the best roadgoing rally car. Countless manufacturers were serving up everything from high-powered wagons to hyperactive hot hatches. Best of all, in the U.K. at least, secondhand cars were fantastically cheap and accessible, even old supercars.

At the time, living hand to mouth simply trying to get the show done, we didn’t realize how lucky we were, though I hope we made the most of the luck that came our way. The reports of ever-­bigger audiences seemed abstract and unbelievable. Only when it became harder and harder to find any country in the world where our filming presence wouldn’t attract a large and excitable crowd did we start to realize that perhaps this stupid show of ours was catching on.

Nonetheless, we rarely had time to rest on our laurels. Indeed, Andy Wilman actively tried to stop us from becoming full of ourselves by, among other things, stridently discouraging attempts to make our disgustingly shabby offices nicer. He believed we had a job to do, and that job was to make an hour of entertainment for Sunday nights on BBC television. The rest was an implausible-­sounding bonus. And perhaps by dint of not trying too hard to be globally appealing, Top Gear became a worldwide phenomenon of the Aughts and beyond. It really couldn’t have happened at any other time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your matter if you haven't already.

Industry observers note that but it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand fresh quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

It has been revealed that this exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into noted dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

It has been revealed that but you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

An Empty EV Tried To Park Itself 868 Times In One Night. The Video Is Hilarious

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event.
  • Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.
  • According to recent reports, an apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event. Maybe you overshot the turn and pulled just a little bit too close to the car next to you. So you back out, adjust, and try again. It's not all that embarrassing—at least not the first time. But how many times does it have to happen before you start to go red in the face (or just give up and drive away)?

Two? Five? What about 868? Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.

According to recent reports, an apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province. The car can be seen on video moving around a small area of the garage. Reversing into a space, pulling forward, repositioning, and doing it all over again.

In a recent development, watching the footage is a bit confusing. If you know that it's a car with parking assist or other autonomy features, you probably assume that the car is just having trouble deciding how well it's parked—like it's some sort of programming error that makes the car's software lack confidence that its parking job is good enough. That may not have been the case here.

It turns out that this particular car wasn't alone in its parking shenanigans. In fact, other video footage soon emerged showing other Avatr and Huajing-branded cars pulling off similar parking stunts.

While the exact reasoning for the repeated parking is unknown, CarNewsChina promptly put together that the cars in the videos all sport Huawei's driver assistance software.

Sources indicate that the footage emerged just as a contest run by Huawei was taking place. It ran through November 13th and was meant to show off the capabilities of the tech organization's Qiankun Intelligent Driving system by giving customers points in eight different categories depending on how they used vehicles' Qiankun-backed features while driving.

Sources indicate that one of these categories is called "Parking Elite." It measures the use of Automatic Parking Assist, Exit-and-Park Assist, Parking Lot Navigation Assist, and Remote Parking Assist to assign points to drivers. The top 100 drivers would receive Huawei points, which can be redeemed for in-app purchases and discounts.

Of course, this reportedly led to some drivers attempting to game the system. CarNewsChina even surfaces a post where one driver claims to have completed 1,000 parking sessions in a single day. It's worth noting that Huawei's tech is technically a driver-assistance feature and not an autonomous driving function; the car is supposed to always have a human supervising these types of actions.

These are just theories, of course, but the claims from drivers and security camera footage do seem like gaming the system is a plausible explanation.

Either way, you have to admit that if you saw a car parking itself 868 times overnight into various parking spaces, you'd wonder what was going on—I know I would. At least it's good for a laugh and didn't cause a traffic jam.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed.
  • Revision 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.
  • Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller patch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Revision 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller patch. When Battlefield Studios confirmed it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a major focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Sources indicate that interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

It has been revealed that and, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you ask the auto industry, subscriptions are the future.
  • In a recent development, A new law aims to put a stop to many forms of in-car subscriptions and after-sale purchases, meaning that if all it takes is a credit card number to switch on a feature after you buy the car, it probably isn't going to fly in New York State.
  • Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law a bill that prohibits automakers, dealerships, and third-party providers from charging car buyers ongoing subscription fees in certain cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you ask the auto industry, subscriptions are the future. Consumers might disagree. They don't want basic features like heated seats being locked behind a paywall, especially when the hardware is already installed. Legislators in Newly introduced York have decided those types of subscriptions are nothing more than a money grab.

In a recent development, A new law aims to put a stop to many forms of in-car subscriptions and after-sale purchases, meaning that if all it takes is a credit card number to switch on a feature after you buy the car, it probably isn't going to fly in New York State. But there are, of course, some exclusions.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law a bill that prohibits automakers, dealerships, and third-party providers from charging car buyers ongoing subscription fees in certain cases. Specifically, it prohibits recurring fees for hardware already installed in the car at the time of purchase, so long as those features don't create an ongoing cost for the manufacturer or a provider.

A snippet from the State's announcement says it best (and uses the infamous heated seat subscription as a prime example):.

Amid rising consumer prices, the upcoming law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.

There are, of course, provisions in the legislation of what features aren't covered by the subscription freeze.

Fresh York notes that driver assistance and automation features, connected cellular services, in-car hotspot, satellite radio, vehicle telematics, roadside assistance, navigation updates, and infotainment features are some of the items excluded from protection under the new legislation.

It has been revealed that notably, that means Tesla can continue charging for features like Full Self-Driving. It does, however, call into question features like Acceleration Boost, which is a $2,000 software-based performance upgrade that requires no extra ongoing costs.

In a recent development, this distinction tracks fairly in line with what both enthusiasts and consumers have been shouting at their phone screens for the last few years. If it's local hardware that's already installed in the vehicle and requires no ongoing costs to maintain (like heated seats, climate control, or remote start using a physical key fob), it feels like a cash grab to continue to charge owners after purchasing the vehicle. Things that cost money to provide—like internet-connected streaming features or driver assistance features that are being actively developed and upgraded over the air—are a bit more defensible.

If your $70,000 SUV still needs its manufacturer's servers, cellular network, fresh maps with to-the-minute traffic conditions, and continuously updated self-driving software—you might not get out of paying a monthly fee. But if it just needs a relay flipped on to work completely offline, then the manufacturer better just work it into the cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hyundai’s fresh IONIQ 3 checks all the boxes as an affordable EV: it offers over 300 miles of range, a practical interior, and Hyundai’s new Pleos infotainment system. So, will Hyundai bring it to the US?

The Hyundai IONIQ 3 is now on sale across Europe and the UK as a smaller sibling to the IONIQ 5, positioned between the Inster EV and Hyundai Kona Electric.

Although it’s part of the IONIQ sub-brand, the IONIQ 3 features a newly introduced “Aero Hatch” design. The new look “reimagines the compact EV silhouette,” Hyundai said, designed to optimize efficiency and interior space.

The response so far has been “extraordinary,” Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, noted after launching the IONIQ 3 last month.

According to Andrew, the compact EV received “more customers registering their interest before launch than any new Hyundai we’ve introduced in the UK,” and that’s including gas-powered and electric vehicles.

The first reviews of the IONIQ 3 have been overwhelmingly positive, highlighting its efficiency, practical interior, and affordable price tag.

A post shared by KindelAuto (@kindelauto).

According to recent reports, so why doesn’t Hyundai sell it in the US? The IONIQ 3 was recently captured driving in public in the US, raising speculation, or perhaps hope, that it will come to the States after all.

The model spotted in the images from KindelAuto is the IONIQ 3 N Line, a sportier, higher-priced trim.

While it’s among the first sightings in the US, we have seen several Hyundai Motor Group electric vehicles testing in the US that are still not available and likely won’t ever be, such as Kia’s EV5 SUV and PV5 van.

The IONIQ 3 is built at Hyundai Motor’s Izmit, Turkey, plant and is specifically designed for European drivers.

We’ve reached out to Hyundai to see if anything has changed, but we haven’t heard back yet. We’ll enhancement you when we hear more.

In Europe and the UK, Hyundai offers the IONIQ 3 with two battery packs: 42 kWh and 61 kWh. The base IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the 42 kWh battery starts at £18,495 ($25,000) OTR and offers up to 213 miles of WLTP range. That’s including the UK’s £3,750 Electric Car Grant.

Industry observers note that the IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery starts at £21,995 ($29,000) and offers a “class-leading” WLTP range of up to 308 miles. That also includes the UK government ECG grant.

Measuring 4,155 mm (163.5″) long, 1,800 mm (70.9″) wide, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) high, with a wheelbase of 2,680 mm (105.5″), Hyundai’s electric hatch is even smaller than the Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.3.

The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its latest Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Hyundai’s newly introduced system is more like using a smartphone. It’s based on the Android Automotive OS with apps and customizable screens, similar to Tesla models. It’s available in the IONIQ 3 with a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Sources indicate that unlike the larger IONIQ 5, the IONIQ 3 uses a 400V architecture. However, the 42 kWh battery can still recharge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes. The 61 kWh battery takes around 30 minutes.

In Germany and other European markets, Hyundai’s compact IONIQ 3 starts at about €28,950 ($33,000).

While Hyundai at the moment has no aims to bring the IONIQ 3 to the US, it does sell the IONIQ 5, built at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside Savannah, GA, alongside the three-row IONIQ 9.

Starting at about $35,000, Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 has remained among the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside of the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

In fact, Hyundai was just named the “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” by US News & World Report for the first time for 2027.

Too bad Tesla refuses to build something like this. Ford could also make a similar car and bring back the Focus nameplate. I don't understand their management decisions.

Hyundai’s sister organization, Kia, also launched the 2027 EV3, which is now on sale starting at just $29,890 in the US.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s still a lot that Porsche won’t divulge about its forthcoming 2028 718 Boxster EV, including horsepower, battery capacity, range, pricing, or even its final, un-camouflaged looks. But after some seat time around the handling course at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we now know what it feels like at—and a little bit beyond—its cornering limits.

Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle.

In other words, this fresh EV feels like a mid-engine Boxster, because that’s where the weight is concentrated. Other than some hypercars, such as the Rimac Nevera, the forthcoming electric Boxster rides atop one of the first EV platforms built around a two-seat sports car. The 800-volt battery pack lives entirely behind the passenger cabin, in the place the engine used to reside, which leads to a 40/60 front/rear weight distribution, similar to the gas-powered Boxster’s 45/55 split. And since there’s no battery under the floor, you sit as low as you would in any other sports car.

See all results for upcoming 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 85009.

We drove what will become the top Boxster model when it goes on sale after its formal debut in early 2027, but Porsche wouldn’t confirm what it will be called. S? GTS? These models wear Pirelli P Zero R Elect tires—and for the first time—mount on staggered-diameter wheels just like the latest 911. The tires measure 255/35ZR-20 up front and 305/30ZR-21 in back, which is more meat than even the last 718 Spyder RS. The company isn’t saying how much power this Boxster’s single rear motor will make—all electric Boxsters will be rear-drive only—but they do claim the sprint to 60 mph will require less than 3.0 seconds. After experiencing being pinned to the seat by a few launch-control starts, the new Boxster feels every bit that quick.

Porsche says this will be the quickest, most powerful Boxster with the highest cornering and braking performance, with a center of gravity that’s—no surprise—much lower than before. We can attest to feeling tons of grip, but can we feel the EV’s added weight? As the Boxster slithered through transitions and dove into apexes, we can’t say it felt heavy, although the squealing from its wide tires sounded at times more tortured than those we recall from the just-over-3000-pound gas-powered Boxster. Porsche says the Boxster EV’s curb weight will fall somewhere within that of the 911 lineup, which ranges from the 3350-pound Carrera to the 4000-pound Turbo S Cabriolet. Here’s hoping it’s toward the lower end of that range, which would be very light for an EV.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 85009.

According to recent reports, while this newly introduced electric version looks like a Boxster and the low seating position feels like a Boxster, with a forward view of a rapidly disappearing hood, Porsche wanted to add some more nostalgic tie-ins by way of fabricated engine noises and simulated shifts. The Taycan got a similar E-Shift feature earlier this year, but while the Taycan’s engine noises weren’t modeled after a specific engine, the Boxster’s very much pays homage to its past. The Boxster’s E-Shift, which is controlled by a knob on the steering wheel and can shift automatically or be controlled by steering wheel paddles, mimics the 981 Boxster GTS’s 3.4-liter flat-six, which Porsche engineers say is the high-water mark for flat-six wails. They told us emissions compromises to the most recent flat-sixes made them choose that one from circa 2015. That mentioned, there’s a bit of revisionist history going on with the electric Boxster’s 8000-rpm “redline” versus the actual 7600-rpm redline in its 981 muse. Either way, the noise emanating from the two speakers—one inside the cabin, one outside—absolutely sounds like a flat-six.

Although the synthesized sound is a solid re-creation, we do think it would be easy to identify the real from the facsimile in a blindfolded test. There’s a lot of nuance going on in the sounds of a flat-six belting to redline—intake and exhaust noise, valve and other mechanical clatter—and it’s hard to generate all of that from a couple speakers. That said, after doing a few hot laps with the system on, we believe it adds to the experience, and it felt weird to switch over to silent and shift-free lapping. We think we’d use this more in a sports car like the Boxster than in the four-door Taycan sedan.

Sources indicate that what else did we learn? As before, the 983 Boxster has both front and rear trunks, and its NACS charge port, which is hidden behind a powered door in the middle of the rear bumper, is the first from Porsche to accommodate both AC and DC charging. Today’s Cayenne and Taycan electrics have separate ports for AC and DC with the NACS only handling DC charging.

Officially, there won’t be any gas-powered Boxster variants, but who knows what the lifecycle might hold, especially if early sales disappoint. After all, remember when the previous generation went four-cylinder only, but then the flat-six made a reappearance a few years later? While we’re as sad as anyone to see the flat-six and manual transmission leave the Boxster lineup, we think that anyone who drives the new one will agree it’s a great-handling sports car.
