Tech Report: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings.
  • Industry observers note that as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically.
  • Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a newly introduced study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, newly introduced research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

Industry observers note that as larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a newly introduced study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body.

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

According to recent reports, rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health.

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health matter.

Industry observers note that in 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the Fresh England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

In a recent development, however, an vital question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The latest findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," stated Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue.".

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

Sources indicate that "Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

In a recent development, the Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," remarked Head-Gordon.

Industry observers note that the implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

According to recent reports, "This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts.".

Recent findings suggest that by revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a newly introduced dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have a real soft spot for weird side quests, and The Final Flush in GTA 6 is about as weird as they come. It's one of the game's Strangers & Freaks missions, and it lives up to that name in every way. It's entirely optional, but it rewards you with a permanent stamina increase. That means you can run, swim and do all sorts of other exhausting activities for longer before running out of breath. On top of that, it's quick, it can be finished in one go, and it's quite honestly hilarious.

The mission puts you in touch with Dr. Merle, a conspiracy theorist who is convinced that Leonida's poop isn't actually going into the sewers. You can start it from Chapter 1 onwards, as either Lucia or Jason, and the stamina boost goes to whichever character you're playing as at the time. It also counts toward the Strangers & Freaks trophy and achievement, so completionists will want to tick it off anyway.

It has been revealed that as is usually the case with the Strangers & Freaks missions, The Final Flush doesn't just show up on your map. You have to go looking for it first. What you're after is a handmade “No Flushers” poster with a QR code on it, and fittingly, these are put up near bathrooms all over Leonida. One reliable spot is the bathroom block at the northern tip of Corsair Key in Mariana County, just north-east of Key Lento. Since it's the only building on Corsair Key, it's very hard to miss, but you can also find posters in the campground area on the east side of Watson Bay and near the Paradise Garage.

Once you've found one, scan the QR code with the WAiNK IT app on your phone. Shortly after, an Automated Machine will text you and ask you to reply "TRUTH" to join the No Flushers movement. Pick the "Truth" reply, and you'll get a second message telling you to meet up at Frank's Waffles in Vice City, along with a code you'll need later on: 00-00-02. The mission will then be marked on your map, and the fun can begin, at last.

Frank's Waffles is in the Tequesta neighborhood of Vice City. Once you're inside, you'll find a man muttering to himself in one of the booths closest to the toilets. One thing to keep in mind, though, is that he seems to only turn up at night. If the mission icon has a padlock on it, simply come back once the sun has gone down (I trust that there are more than enough sidemissions in Leonida to keep you occupied until then).

In a recent development, when you get close, he rapidly covers up whatever he's working on, tells you he's holding a royal flush and asks if you have a "coda" for that. Interact with him to bring up the dialogue options, then pick the code option. The man turns out to be Dr. Merle, and his theory is that Leonida's waste is secretly being sent to a government facility that siphons DNA from it. To prove it, he swallows a tracking device and heads straight into the bathroom to send it on its way through the pipes. It's not the most glamorous proposal, but you have to admire his commitment.

Once Dr. Merle has finished his business, follow him outside and get into his van. There's no proper objective marker on this drive, so you'll need to listen quite closely to his directions. Head south first, turn east at the intersection he points out, and from there, just keep following the highway. Eventually, he'll lead you to a sewage treatment plant, tell you where to park along the coast, and you can follow him on foot toward the facility.

Sources indicate that when you reach the fence, Dr. Merle starts working on a metal gate and asks you to keep watch. Keep an eye on the road on the other side of the gate, because a van will soon pull up, and the driver will want to know what exactly you're doing there. Focus on him and choose the "Defuse" option, which has you claim you're simply fixing the gate. He'll take your word for it and drive off again, which is tremendously lucky for both of you.

It has been revealed that once you're inside the grounds, you'll need to find the tracker, so head toward the area highlighted on your map. Along the way, you'll come across two workers having a chat. You can carefully sneak past them, or, if they ask whether you're the electricians, use the "Lie" option and play along. Either way, go through the open metal gate to their left, bear slightly right, and you'll find a set of double doors that lead into the building.

According to recent reports, inside, Dr. Merle quite understandably starts to panic, because the tracker is apparently right below your feet, and there's no obvious way to reach it. Head up the metal stairs in the room and you'll find a control panel on the platform above, which you can interact with using Triangle/Y. To open the way down, all three lights on the left-hand side of the panel need to be green. Press the buttons next to the two red lights (the middle and bottom ones), then tilt the main lever. A hidden staircase will open up right where Dr. Merle is sitting, so head back down and follow him.

In a recent development, downstairs, you'll find a large and rather mysterious-looking chamber, and Dr. Merle, determined to prove his theory right, climbs straight in. As it starts filling with liquid, he asks you to flush him, so press the red button on the control panel in front of the chamber. That, unsurprisingly, gets the attention of the water authority. A voice over the loudspeaker warns you that the authorities are on their way, and that the chamber is highly toxic, so you absolutely should not get inside.

Recent findings suggest that you should get inside anyway. Step into the chamber and you'll be flushed automatically, which technically counts as a crime, so don't be alarmed when the "Crime Committed" notice pops up. After a fade to black, you'll wake up back at home (how you pull of that feat exactly is anyone's guess), with a notification telling you that your max stamina has increased. There are no side effects whatsoever, and the mission is complete.

Sources indicate that running away is technically an option, though not a particularly good one. You'll still be reported for trespassing, the police will swarm the facility, and you'll have a chase on your hands on your way out. On top of that, there's no reward for bailing, so you'll miss out on the stamina boost. Truth be told, it's a pretty easy decision: a quick trip through some toxic sludge is a small price to pay for a permanent upgrade.

As for Dr. Merle, nobody quite knows where he ended up. I just hope he found his DNA siphoning center.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hoYoverse just wrapped up a significant Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

According to recent reports, the upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the massive new world headlining Version 4.0.

According to recent reports, planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

According to recent reports, the imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Sources indicate that much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

Sources indicate that as you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two newly introduced 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

Recent findings suggest that when you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

Industry observers note that she also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

It has been revealed that version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

It has been revealed that finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be declared at a later date.

  • On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No.
  • It has been revealed that although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

It has been revealed that although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon.

It has been revealed that NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

Industry observers note that bilibili Gaming beat Gen.G in Brooklyn to win the 2026 League of Legends World Championship, the LPL's first world title since 2021. Added to their First Stand trophy, the result gives a Chinese side a double that no team had managed since 2016, just as Riot takes the 2027 season opener to China.

Bilibili Gaming are world champions. The LPL side needed four games to beat Gen.G in Latest York and win the club’s first Worlds title. The result ends a run of four straight LCK world titles. It also gives the LPL its first world crown since EDward Gaming won in 2021.

BLG took the hardest possible route. They knocked out all four LCK teams at the event: Hanwha Life Esports, Dplus KIA, T1 and Gen.G. Every Korean side that travelled to the tournament went home after facing them.

Industry observers note that the final turned early. BLG levelled the series at 1-1 by winning a 53-minute second game. It was the longest game of the whole tournament. Gen.G had reached the final with two 3-0 knockout wins, over LYON on 4 November and Invictus Gaming on 7 November.

According to recent reports, for Knight, the MVP award closes a loop. The BLG mid laner lost the 2024 final to T1. Two years later, he finished on the winning side.

Industry observers note that the runners-up looked inward after the defeat. At Gen.G’s post-final press conference, Chovy said the team had broken its own rules. Duro, playing his first Worlds, regretted that they had dropped their drafting proposal.

According to recent reports, gen.G still leave with US$800,000 as runners-up. Semi-finalists T1 and Invictus Gaming received US$400,000 each. Riot ran the event from 15 October to 14 November with 19 teams.

In a recent development, gen.G’s admission points to the draft as a weak spot. The figures support a narrower reading too. Gen.G swept both knockout opponents before the final. Against BLG, they could not hold the lead after taking the opening game.

According to recent reports, worlds was BLG’s second international trophy of the year. In March they won the First Stand Tournament in São Paulo. They beat G2 Esports 3-1 in that final and collected the US$250,000 top prize.

Winning both events makes BLG the first team since SK Telecom T1 in 2016 to take more than one major international title in a year.

Industry observers note that our first Summoner’s Cup. It’s finally coming home.

The 2027 Mid-Season Invitational will be held in Valencia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward latest ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

In a recent development, "These findings break upcoming ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," mentioned Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.".

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's.

Industry observers note that more than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an key role in how the disease develops.

Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is key for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role.

Recent findings suggest that "Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," stated Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are crucial findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.".

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the upcoming research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

Industry observers note that that distinction could be vital for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential Fresh Target for Alzheimer's Treatments.

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," noted Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.".

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an vital opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a upcoming position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical tech giant Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration.".

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal.

In a recent development, the research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who states participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his intends for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science.".

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.

This narrative-driven puzzler is all about becoming a parent, losing yourself, being exhausted, and trying to find your own way to heal. The gameplay is a mix of almost comic book-like stories to scroll through and puzzles that make sense if you look around for a bit.

Recent findings suggest that escape the Baby Alarm is all about discovering who you are after having a baby, finding your own voice, and making sure that you are reflecting on your own self as well, so that you can be the best version of yourself. Industry observers note that download now! Escape the Baby Alarm.

GTA 6: Red Hulk Quest Guide

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While many of Grand Theft Auto 6’s craziest moments happen out of the blue while freeroaming, others are rewards for helping out strangers with their extended questlines.
  • One such questline centers around the strawberry farmer Kyle McKittrick, a man who needs a hand or two ensuring that his special growth formula wins the local strawberry competition.
  • Sources indicate that kyle’s questline can be started as early as Chapter 1, provided you spot his Snapmatic post while scrolling as Jason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many of Grand Theft Auto 6’s craziest moments happen out of the blue while freeroaming, others are rewards for helping out strangers with their extended questlines. These questlines can be picked up in a variety of ways, rewarding players for scrolling Snapmatic or keeping an open eye around the world.

One such questline centers around the strawberry farmer Kyle McKittrick, a man who needs a hand or two ensuring that his special growth formula wins the local strawberry competition. As is GTA tradition, this simple premise spirals quickly, giving a glimpse of Rockstar’s take on a Marvel legend, but only if you can find him.

Sources indicate that kyle’s questline can be started as early as Chapter 1, provided you spot his Snapmatic post while scrolling as Jason. Look for a post featuring a prop plane and open it to get the quest marker far to the north of the Keys. This is a major detour from any of the story content in Chapter 1, so don’t worry about waiting, Kyle isn’t going anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that when you have time, drive up to his farm, and he’ll ask whichever protagonist you’re playing to pilot his prop plane and douse his strawberry fields with his own blend of growth hormones. This is a super chill mission, all you need to do is dump the chemicals above where Kyle is parked, dousing both him and his strawberries on each run. He’ll pay you for your help and ask you to keep in touch for any updates.

Sources indicate that after around 24 hours in-game, Kyle will call Jason and Lucia, asking them to pick up a supply of chemicals from a local biker gang. Once you arrive at the marked location, you’ll call him again for some extra context. He explains that the bikers will be expecting payment, but he doesn’t care how you get the chems either way.

The goal is to leave the compound with the van filled with Kyle’s chemicals, all else is secondary. At first, the bikers will demand $5,000 for the van, but it can be easily bartered down to $3,000. Refusing their price will start a fight, and it can be difficult to get the van off the premises with a sea of angry bikers.

I’d recommend paying the bartered-down cost if you can afford it, allowing you to safely drive the van out and park it at Kyle’s to complete the quest.

Wait a bit longer for another message from Kyle, or keep an eye on his Snapmatic account for a video where he demonstrates off his insanely massive strawberries before running off camera. Return to Kyle’s farm one final time to find an armed outfit of government agents attempting to get him to come outside.

To sneak in, enter the chemical van parked nearby, where you can slip on a hazmat suit to blend into the crowd. Head behind the barn and two guards will escort you inside, revealing Kyle’s new, Hulkish form. He’ll throw open the doors of the barn, and the assembled agents will open fire.

In a recent development, if you do nothing, Kyle will die, so take out the two guards still beside you in the barn and assist Kyle with clearing the rest. Once you do, he’ll fall to his knees, where you can comfort him and give him a hug for a huge boost in Professional Criminal Profile points.

It has been revealed that after you calm him down, Kyle will leap off, surely to assist against a future alien invasion of some kind. Thus ends one of Grand Theft Auto 6’s wildest questlines, shifting from farming assistance to superhero origin story at the drop of a hat.

#110091. AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis.
  • The newly introduced approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

The newly introduced approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records.

Recent findings suggest that under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

Sources indicate that confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

Sources indicate that the researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases.

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

In a recent development, the AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

In a recent development, for example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

It has been revealed that another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

A Fresh Approach to Early Cancer Screening.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

Industry observers note that for example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, stated: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 fresh cases diagnosed in 2022.".

According to recent reports, "Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research demonstrates that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods.".

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

According to recent reports, dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved.".

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages.".

More Research Needed Before Clinical Use.

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's key to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

Sources indicate that "But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions.".

Sources indicate that the findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EDward Gaming have lost captain nobody and CHICHOO, two days after releasing Smoggy to Bilibili Gaming. The VCT China partner team must now rebuild before the China Kickoff in Hangzhou in January.

EDward Gaming have parted ways with CHICHOO and captain nobody, two pillars of the side that won VALORANT Champions 2024. Both players left the VCT China partner team on the same day. EDG unveiled both exits on Weibo. Their exits end a five-year spell at the organisation.

The departures follow rapidly on from Smoggy’s move to Bilibili Gaming. Within a week, three players had gone from the EDG roster. No replacements have been named.

Wang ‘nobody’ Senxu joined EDG on 7 September 2021. He served as the team’s captain and in-game leader. He had started out as the side’s Initiator before taking on those leadership duties. CHICHOO, whose full name is Wan Shunzhi, played the Controller role. Alongside CHICHOO, he formed the core of the only Chinese team to win Champions. That title, sealed on 25 August 2024, made EDG the first organisation from China, and from Asia, to lift the trophy. The team’s total winnings stand at roughly $1,592,287.

It has been revealed that the pair were still central to the side in 2026. At Masters London, CHICHOO and nobody each played 12 maps. Their average combat scores were 179 and 184 respectively. EDG finished third in London and earned $125,000. Their run ended with a 0-3 defeat to Leviatán in the lower bracket final on 20 June 2026.

Where nobody goes next is not yet confirmed. Sheep Esports reported, citing sources, that he is expected to join Trace Esports for 2027. Trace’s Kai and deLb are said to be under contract until the end of 2027. If that move happens, nobody and Smoggy would both start the latest season with different organisations.

It has been revealed that the timing is awkward for EDG. The organisation was named a VCT partner team on 21 October, on a two-year contract. That deal now begins with a heavily changed roster.

According to recent reports, the China Kickoff is an S-Tier LAN event. It is organised by TJ Sports, Hero Esports and Riot Games. The league’s partner sides make up eight places in the field, with the remaining four split evenly between visiting teams and open qualifier entrants. EDG will need a settled line-up in place to compete there.

#110088. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1338 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed.
  • Sources indicate that for years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works.
  • But the latest findings raise an vital question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A upcoming study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

Sources indicate that for years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the latest findings raise an vital question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a upcoming study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity.".

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI.

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," claims Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story.

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

Sources indicate that AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly key as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

According to recent reports, "The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," indicates Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior.

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

It has been revealed that developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

Sources indicate that the concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain.

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

It has been revealed that "Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," indicates Kar. "This is especially key for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline.".

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is key for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a latest approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as vital.

The discovery could help guide the development of a fresh generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

#110085. Tech Report: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1602 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to fresh research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20.
  • In a recent development, the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to fresh research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History.

Industry observers note that published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

It has been revealed that the scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how swiftly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

In a recent development, AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

It has been revealed that scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

According to recent reports, for the newly introduced analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades.

The results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each upcoming mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

In a recent development, researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more rapidly.

Sources indicate that this consistency could have important medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

A Hidden Warning Sign of Leukemia.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

In a recent development, in at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep.".

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer highlighted the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.".

Sources indicate that he added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.".

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Industry observers note that dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

Sources indicate that "As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study demonstrates that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.".

Recent findings suggest that watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

Recent findings suggest that she added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.".

Years of Blood Samples Unlock Upcoming Cancer Clues.

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

"While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.".

The women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

It has been revealed that the findings also demonstrated that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

A Newly introduced Path Toward Preventing Leukemia.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Stepping up to replace Huang for the immediate future is current Nvidia executive vice president and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who is becoming interim CEO on top of her established number-crunching duties.

One would assume she's quickly calculated just how much extra work Jensen's alleged inability to not get amorous with women who aren't his wife will add to her plate until a permanent successor is found. Speaking of that, Nvidia wrote that they "will consider internal and external candidates" in their scanning for someone to step into Huang's leather jacket. Actually, Nvidia folks, maybe don't let the upcoming person wear the leather jacket, lest people potentially find them dangerously attractive. Failing that, maybe a pair of padlocked underpants are in order, adorned with flashing green lights to ensure brand recognition in trouserless scenarios.

The tech giant's board of directors have gone ahead and appointed Harvey Jones as their first ever chairperson, one would assume to help convince money people that they've got strong enough leadership in place until their new permanent boss is found.

"Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," interim CEO Kress remarked "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders." Oh, come on, think how many people would cheer if you said you fancied pivoting even a tiny bit of attention away from AI and back to consumer GPUs.

"Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound," the company's release concluded. "Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.".

Sources indicate that goodbye, leather jacket man who was allegedly too sexy for his own good, despite being a nerd who stands on stages waving hardware about. Odds are we'll see you again, possibly in the company of Elon Musk, because execs can never be allowed to be out of lucrative work for more than five minutes.

  • It's not all sunshine and roses, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Space, the final frontier. And like all frontiers, there's always someone willing to take a chance on building a fresh life there, no matter how much of a ludicrously ill-advised idea it may be. It's a concept that offers rich ground for colony management sims, but there haven't been many options for that on mobile, well, until Ember Outpost arrived.

Available now on iOS and Android, Ember Outpost is a colony management sim that sees you guiding a group of settlers on an alien world. Everything, from food to water and other supplies, will need to be crafted or collected, and you'll also have to deal with the drastically contradictory personalities of your colonists. Oh, and let's add natural disasters and murderous raiders, just for some extra spice.

It's not all sunshine and roses, though. Ember Outpost does have the lingering spectre of AI in some bizarrely high-res assets scattered throughout, and promotional imagery. Which is a shame because I think part of the appeal of colony sims such as RimWorld is how easily readable and minimalist they are. But you can't have everything.

Recent findings suggest that for what it is, Ember Outpost offers exactly what those who want RimWorld on mobile have been waiting for. Densely detailed colony sim action, where there's just as much potential for disasters inside the walls of your compound as outside of it.

If you think you might like to practice a little before taking your foray into the great unknown, then why not check out some of our choice picks of the best strategy games on Android?

Download now! Ember Outpost: Colony Sim.
