Breaking: 10 Fighting Game Remakes That Improved Everything From The Original Games

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I still look back fondly on those afternoons at my grandmother's house, sitting in front of the TV with my cousins and firing up my PlayStation 1 for hours of fighting games like Tekken 3—a series I'm still playing with Tekken 8—and Mortal Kombat Trilogy, one of the best games with non-stop violence that ever existed.
  • Still, the genre hasn't always been perfect.
  • Fortunately, some of those games got a second chance through exceptional remakes that fixed every flaw from the originals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I still look back fondly on those afternoons at my grandmother's house, sitting in front of the TV with my cousins and firing up my PlayStation 1 for hours of fighting games like Tekken 3—a series I'm still playing with Tekken 8—and Mortal Kombat Trilogy, one of the best games with non-stop violence that ever existed.

Still, the genre hasn't always been perfect. Plenty of classics introduced with serious balance challenges, rough performance, or questionable mechanics that could easily sour the experience.

Fortunately, some of those games got a second chance through exceptional remakes that fixed every flaw from the originals. Here are 10 fighting games that completely reinvented themselves with new mechanics, features and definitive balancing.

As a longtime JoJo's Bizarre Adventure fan, I was excited when All-Star Battle got its Western PS3 release in 2014 (following its 2013 Japanese debut). That hype faded fast once I felt its 30 fps frame rate, slower combat pacing, and a Campaign mode weighed down by stamina timers and microtransactions.

According to recent reports, in 2022, Bandai Namco released JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: All-Star Battle R on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S, Switch, and PC. While the Switch version runs at 30 fps, the PlayStation, Xbox, and PC editions target 60 fps, immediately making combat feel snappier to me. It also added an Assist system for extending combos and expanded the roster across the series.

Recent findings suggest that best of all, it dropped the original Campaign's stamina timers and energy purchases—though the game still features paid DLC characters and costumes, and solo players lost the original Story and Campaign modes in favor of the panel-based All-Star Battle mode. For me, the faster gameplay made that trade-off worth it.

Sources indicate that not every necessary remake is modern. While the 1993 arcade Virtua Fighter was a landmark title, its 1994 Sega Saturn port was rough, with flat, untextured polygonal models and distracting polygon flickering.

Sources indicate that released in 1995 for arcades and the Saturn, Virtua Fighter Remix tackled those early-port challenges head-on. Side by side on Saturn, the jump is clear: Remix introduced texture-mapped character models with far sharper facial and outfit detail. It wasn't a flawless fix—some polygon glitches remained, the lighting shifted, and load times increased—but for Saturn owners at the time, it was still a major visual upgrade that stood up much better alongside early Tekken.

After falling in love with Bloody Roar 2, playing Bloody Roar 3 on PS2 (following its 2000 arcade debut) left me wanting more. Its animal-transformation premise was still a blast, but to my eyes, the early-PS2 visuals looked rough, with jagged edges and coarse textures.

Recent findings suggest that in 2002, Bloody Roar: Primal Fury rolled out on Nintendo GameCube (followed by Bloody Roar Extreme on Xbox in 2003) as an enhanced remake of Bloody Roar 3. Compared to the PS2 release, the GameCube version offered cleaner character models, upgraded lighting, animated endings for the cast, and newcomers like Cronos and Ganesha. Personally, it became my go-to way to play the game, making every match feel far more polished and satisfying.

Sources indicate that I've loved Street Fighter for years, but jumping into specific Western arcade revisions of 1994's Super Street Fighter II Turbo—notably the World 940223 and USA 940323 builds—was a rude awakening. Both are notorious for a difficulty bug that makes the CPU unusually fierce regardless of the machine's setting, on top of lopsided matchups involving Old Sagat, Vega, and a tournament-banned Akuma.

Sources indicate that when Super Street Fighter II Turbo HD Remix hit PS3 and Xbox 360 in 2008, I was immediately won over. Udon Entertainment redrew the sprites and stages in HD, and the game added a rebalanced mode to rein in dominant fighters while still letting purists play under the original rules. Paired with built-in GGPO rollback netcode, it became a much friendlier way to enjoy a classic.

The PS2 introduced me to countless classics, including Dead or Alive 2: Hardcore (an updated PS2 edition of the 1999 arcade and 2000 Dreamcast fighter). I loved its fast pace and multi-tiered stages, though its early-PS2 visuals aged swiftly and its counter-heavy combat could feel unforgiving.

According to recent reports, dead or Alive Ultimate arrived on the original Xbox in 2004 with a ground-up remake of DOA2 built on an upgraded DOA3 engine. Compared to the PS2 version, the leap in lighting, textures, and stage detail was night and day. While reversals remained a defining—and sometimes divisive—part of the formula, Ultimate felt like the definitive package, bringing together fighters like Tengu and Bayman alongside DOA3's Hitomi and over 20 interactive stages.

At launch, it also stood out for its Xbox Live lobbies and spectator mode—a huge draw at the time, even though Microsoft officially shut down original Xbox Live servers in April 2010.

In a recent development, SNK's catalog deserves a spot in any fighting game discussion, including The King of Fighters 2002. This fantastic Neo Geo game had strong core gameplay, but its presentation felt more stripped-back to me than SNK's earlier classics, with a soundtrack that didn't hit as hard and several NESTS-saga favorites missing from the roster.

According to recent reports, I also wasn't a fan of a meta dominated by Billy Kane, Athena, and Choi. That's why the 2009 remake, The King of Fighters 2002: Unlimited Match (originally on PS2, later coming to Xbox Live Arcade in 2010 and PC in 2015), felt like such a triumph.

Expanding the roster to 66 playable characters in its console and Xbox Live Arcade editions, it overhauled the stages (using 3D polygonal backgrounds on PS2 and 2D replacements on PC), added a new soundtrack, refined MAX Mode cancels, and introduced new moves across the cast—turning it into one of my favorite 2D fighters SNK has ever made.

Sources indicate that the original Karateka launched in 1984 for the Apple II before receiving ports for Atari 8-bit systems, the NES/Famicom, and the Commodore 64. Its flaws stood out quickly, though: the controls were slow and stiff, there were no checkpoints—meaning a single lost fight sent you right back to the beginning—and the combat system was bare-bones.

In a recent development, in 2012, however, a remake arrived on Xbox 360 before making its way to PC, PS3, and iOS. This latest version rebuilt the visuals from the ground up in cel-shaded 3D powered by Unreal Engine 3, and introduced a one-on-one combat system built around visual and audio cues for countering attacks. What really won me over was how it replaced the single-life structure with three consecutive suitors, each with different speeds and their own unique endings.

At launch, the original Fatal Fury: King of Fighters—released in 1991 for Neo Geo—drew plenty of criticism for offering only three playable characters: Andy Bogard, Terry Bogard, and Joe Higashi. On top of that, its gameplay lacked depth, relying on a simple three-button control scheme.

Recent findings suggest that in 1999, Fatal Fury: Wild Ambition hit the Hyper Neo Geo 64 and PlayStation 1, expanding the roster to 12 fighters in arcades and 14 on PS1. It also introduced latest defensive and meter-management mechanics, including the Heat Meter, Heat Blow, and Overdrive Power. It's worth noting, however, that Sony's console version took several noticeable graphical downgrades compared to the arcade release.

According to recent reports, this title might not be as widely known as others on this list, but it had a strong following in Japan back in the day. Asuka 120% Burning Fest. originally introduced in 1994 for the FM Towns, though several problems held the experience back—including a limited roster, a lack of defensive tools, and the fact that it was locked to a niche Japanese home computer.

According to recent reports, several years later, in 1999, Asuka 120% Final: Burning Fest. Final arrived on PS1. While it remained a Japan-only release, this version featured a completely rebuilt combat engine with a much faster pace and noticeably smoother sprite animations. It also expanded the character roster—adding secret fighters into the mix—and introduced deeper offensive and defensive mechanics, such as air recovery.

According to recent reports, the original Eternal Champions launched on the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive in 1993 in North America, followed by Europe and Japan in 1994. Like many entries on this list, though, it suffered from frustrating complications—including punishing AI, clunky, unintuitive controls, and a small roster, among other flaws.

Sources indicate that it wasn't until 1995 that its remake, Eternal Champions: Challenge from the Dark Side, which can be considered one of the best fighting games stuck on older systems, arrived on the Sega CD as an expanded overhaul of the original. It expanded the starting roster from nine to 13 fighters—alongside a large lineup of unlockables—introduced upcoming FMV finishers called Cinekills, and improved the difficulty curve compared to the original game.

The Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight is set to kick off today at 2pm PT, 5pm ET, 10pm GMT.

Industry observers note that the biggest reason why you might want to tune in is, of course, that a whole chunk of the event will focus on Diablo 4. Blizzard will unveil the second class coming to the game with the Lord of Hatred expansion. The developer, of course, released the first of two classes - Paladin - immediately at the upcoming expansion’s initial reveal back in December.

According to recent reports, lord of Hatred is set to arrive April 28, and there’s even more it’s bringing to the core game that will be shown off during the livestream. Blizzard remarked we can expect a deeper look at the revamped skill trees, as well as endgame mechanics and features Lord of Hatred is set to introduce.

Beyond Diablo 4 itself, the showcase will feature updates on Diablo Immortal, and even Diablo 2: Resurrected. Blizzard hasn’t been teasing any other announcements, but many still hold out hope for a proper Diablo 1 remaster.

As always, you’ll be able to watch the show live on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, and Twitch channels. We’ve embedded the Twitch player below for your convenience.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentinels have signed Briton Georgio 'keiko' Sanassy from NRG as the final starter in their 2027 VCT Americas lineup.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Sentinels lineup for 2027 now reads johnqt, brawk, OXY, canezerra and keiko.
  • Sentinels called keiko ‘bloody brilliant’ in its announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentinels have signed Briton Georgio 'keiko' Sanassy from NRG as the final starter in their 2027 VCT Americas lineup. The move pairs him again with former NRG teammate brawk as Sentinels try to return to international events after missing them all in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the Sentinels lineup for 2027 now reads johnqt, brawk, OXY, canezerra and keiko. Zellsis rounds out the group as sixth man. He came back to the organisation on 7 November in that role and as a content creator. Contract lengths were not disclosed.

Sentinels called keiko ‘bloody brilliant’ in its announcement. Riot’s VALORANT Esports account then shared the news and described him as ‘the finishing touch’ on the lineup.

Sheep Esports first reported the move on 8 November, citing sources, and stated keiko was expected to play controller. The same report had brawk on initiator and johnqt on sentinel.

It has been revealed that the signing ends a rapid rebuild. OXY arrived on 2 November and brawk a day later. canezerra followed on 6 November. Four days after that, cortezia and Reduxx were released.

Only a few hours before joining Sentinels, brawk had ruled out staying at NRG.

keiko’s NRG spell ran from 12 November 2025 to 21 October 2026. He finished third at Masters Santiago 2026. He also placed third in both VCT Americas Stage 1 and Stage 2. At Champions 2026 he finished joint fifth to sixth.

Sources indicate that that spell ended once Champions was over. NRG told him he would not be kept for the following year, keiko said on X on 21 October. He was then free to look for a newly introduced team as a restricted free agent.

Sentinels reached no international event in 2026. The team went out of that year’s Kickoff in the bottom four. It then missed the playoffs in both Stage 1 and Stage 2. Adding a player with that run of results is consistent with a side trying to close the gap promptly.

Industry observers note that keiko was born on 12 September 2003. He grew up in and around London. He played competitive Fortnite before switching to VALORANT. His VALORANT career began at UK sides WYLDE, from May to August 2022, and BONK, from October to December 2022. He then joined Apeks from January to November 2023. That year he won the Challengers Rising Stars award. Team Liquid followed, from November 2023 to November 2025. His move to Sentinels places a British player at the centre of a rebuilt Americas contender.

The final piece has arrived, and he's bloody brilliant@Keikofps is officially a Sentinel pic.twitter.com/F5plGsyugj.

— Sentinels (@Sentinels) November 16, 2026.

Sources indicate that the new lineup’s next test is the Americas Kickoff. Partner teams are guaranteed a place only at Kickoff. The Americas has eight partner teams, and all of them receive direct invitations to its event. Four further places go to non-partner teams.

Industry observers note that the 2027 Kickoff events will be played in person in each international region. One of the non-partner places in the Americas will be decided by a Last Chance Qualifier in São Paulo on 17–18 December.
